title_options: Saudi Arabia Promised a 170 km City. Here's What Satellites Show.

We Checked The Line From Space: 170 km Promised, This Is What's There
items.description:
Saudi Arabia Promised a 170 km City. Here's What Satellites Show.

Saudi Arabia announced a 170 km linear city. We pointed free Sentinel-2 satellite images at the same stretch of desert, year after year (2020-2026), and kept three things apart: what was PROMISED, what was REPORTED, and what we OBSERVED.

CHAPTERS
0:00 170 km promised
0:25 The promise
0:52 What was reported
1:41 How we looked
2:29 What the satellites show
3:09 The dark segment
4:01 Trying to break our own result
5:15 What we cannot say
5:51 Promised, reported, observed

WHAT WE CLAIM, AND HOW SURE WE ARE
- Observed: a straight corridor and a dark segment of about 1.6-1.9 km, measured at 10 m per pixel. A water index reads it as water-like, which is a clue, not proof.
- Not claimed: that the corridor is The Line, that it is a finished city, that the segment grew, or what the segment is.
- Reported items are attributed to the outlets named. We could not open the original Bloomberg, Semafor and Reuters articles from our research setup, so those lines rest on how other outlets described them.

SOURCES (as reported; links are to the pages we actually read)
- C1 Construction Briefing (with Dezeen, AGBI) (2024-04-09): https://www.constructionbriefing.com/8036596.article
- C2 Bloomberg via Dezeen (2024-04-09): https://www.dezeen.com/2024/04/09/the-line-neom-scaled-back-dezeen-agenda/
- C3 Semafor (2026-05-22): https://www.semafor.com/article/05/22/2026/saudis-neom-halts-work-on-the-line-until-after-2030
- C4 Reuters via Seoul Economic Daily (2026-10-13): https://en.sedaily.com/international/2026/10/13/saudi-arabia-shelves-neom-stadium-as-megaproject-unravels

items.title: NASA’s Rover Ran Over a Rock on Mars. This Was Inside.
items.description:
NASA’s Rover Ran Over a Rock on Mars. This Was Inside.

In May 2024, NASA's Curiosity rover drove over a rock in Gediz Vallis channel on Mount Sharp, Mars, and cracked it open. Inside were yellow crystals. The rover's APXS instrument identified them as elemental sulfur, the first pure sulfur ever found on Mars. NASA's project scientist: "It shouldn't be there, so now we have to explain it."

We follow the find with NASA's own images: how the team knew it was sulfur, why it was a surprise, why the stones were invisible from orbit, and what scientists think now.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Yellow crystals on Mars
0:24 The accident
1:25 How they knew it was sulfur
2:01 Why it shouldn't be there
2:45 A whole field, invisible from orbit
3:19 Gediz Vallis channel
3:45 Drill hole #41 at Mammoth Lakes
4:25 What scientists think now
5:30 Not evidence of life
5:57 Where it stands

WHAT IS CONFIRMED, AND WHAT IS NOT
- Confirmed (NASA/JPL): pure elemental sulfur, a whole field of sulfur stones, too brittle to drill; no evidence of volcanoes or hot springs near this part of Mount Sharp.
- Peer reviewed (Science, 2026): the stones appear to have formed in place, roughly 3 billion years ago; the authors PROPOSE magmatic vapor as the source.
- Not peer reviewed (conference abstracts, 2026): an impact-melt idea that depends on a rock layer nobody has measured yet.
- Not claimed: evidence of life. There is no video of the moment the rock cracked; only photos taken afterwards.

SOURCES
- NASA/JPL, "NASA's Curiosity Rover Discovers a Surprise in a Martian Rock" (July 18, 2024): https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/nasas-curiosity-rover-discovers-a-surprise-in-a-martian-rock/
- NASA/JPL, "NASA's Curiosity Mars Rover Takes a Last Look at Mysterious Sulfur" (Nov. 18, 2024): https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/nasas-curiosity-mars-rover-takes-a-last-look-at-mysterious-sulfur/
- VanBommel et al., "A native sulfur deposit in Gale crater, Mars," Science 393, 820-825 (2026), doi:10.1126/science.adu5501: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adu5501
- Washington University in St. Louis release on the Science paper: https://artsci.washu.edu/node/28889
- Rapin et al., EGU26-22162: https://meetingorganizer.copernicus.org/EGU26/EGU26-22162.html
- Maggioni et al., EGU26-12327: https://meetingorganizer.copernicus.org/EGU26/EGU26-12327.html

IMAGES
NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS: PIA26307, PIA26308, PIA26309, PIA26210, PIA26363, PIA26366, PIA26367, PIA26410, PIA26471 (Mastcam, MAHLI).
NASA/JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona: PIA26245 (HiRISE, enhanced color).
Diagrams are OrbitalAtlas schematics, not to scale. Use of NASA imagery does not imply NASA endorsement.

items.title: NASA Changed Its Moon Mission. Here's Why.
title_options: NASA Changed Its Moon Mission. Here's Why.
NASA's Next Moon Mission Won't Go to the Moon
Artemis III: Docking Two Moon Landers - in Earth Orbit
items.description:
NASA Changed Its Moon Mission. Here's Why.

Artemis II flew four astronauts around the Moon in April 2026. The next crew won't go to the Moon at all. On February 27, 2026, NASA turned Artemis III into a 2027 test flight in low Earth orbit and moved the first landing to Artemis IV, targeted for 2028. On October 23, 2026, NASA published the flight plan: about 14 days in orbit, a docking with a Blue Origin lander test article with astronauts going inside, and a nose-to-nose docking with a SpaceX Starship test article that nobody enters.

CHAPTERS
0:00 The Moon mission that stays in Earth orbit
0:38 What NASA changed in February
1:38 The hardware is already real
2:23 The crew
2:56 Three launches
3:17 The orbits
3:44 Docking 1: Blue Moon
4:17 Docking 2: Starship
4:47 Extra tests and splashdown
5:14 Why test this in Earth orbit
5:52 Apollo did this too
6:03 What is still unknown
6:17 The test before the landing

WHAT IS CONFIRMED, AND WHAT IS NOT
- Confirmed (NASA): Artemis III is planned for 2027 in low Earth orbit; about 14 days; Blue Moon test article about 273 miles up; Orion docks beside its crew cabin and up to two astronauts go inside for about two days; Starship test article docks nose to nose for up to two hours, crew does not enter; splashdown in the Pacific off California; crewed landings near the lunar South Pole planned from 2028 (Artemis IV).
- Not announced: a launch date (NASA says 2027), and which lander will carry the first Artemis IV crew.
- Not real footage: every docking is an OrbitalAtlas illustration, labelled on screen. Artemis II photos and video are labelled as Artemis II, not Artemis III.
- The Apollo 9 / Apollo 11 comparison is our historical parallel, not a NASA statement.

SOURCES
- NASA, "NASA Adds Mission to Artemis Lunar Program, Updates Architecture" (Feb 27, 2026): https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-adds-mission-to-artemis-lunar-program-updates-architecture/
- NASA, "NASA's Artemis III Mission to Test Future Moon Lander Operations" (Oct 23, 2026): https://www.nasa.gov/missions/artemis/nasas-artemis-iii-mission-to-test-future-moon-lander-operations/
- NASA, "How NASA's Artemis III Lander Test Will Pave Way for Moon Landings" (Jul 15, 2026): https://www.nasa.gov/directorates/esdmd/artemis-campaign-development-division/human-landing-system-program/how-nasas-artemis-iii-lander-test-will-pave-way-for-moon-landings/
- NASA, "NASA Joins Artemis III Orion Modules; Rocket Hardware Update" (Aug 5, 2026): https://www.nasa.gov/blogs/missions/2026/08/05/nasa-joins-artemis-iii-orion-modules-rocket-hardware-update/
- NASA, "NASA Completes Artemis III Booster Stacking, Shares Status Update" (Oct 13, 2026): https://www.nasa.gov/blogs/missions/2026/10/13/nasa-completes-artemis-iii-booster-stacking-shares-status-update/

items.title: Why Scientists Buried a Telescope Under Antarctica
title_options: Why Scientists Buried a Telescope Under Antarctica
items.description:
Why Scientists Buried a Telescope Under Antarctica

Beneath the South Pole, the IceCube Neutrino Observatory uses Antarctic ice to detect particles from space. We explore the original deep array, how hot-water drilling made its construction possible, and how a rare flash of light can begin a search for a distant source.

This episode distinguishes the original array, completed in 2010, from the upgrade deployed in 2026. Detector graphics are explanatory schematics. Space animations are visualizations. Antarctic traverse footage is contextual field footage, not a record of IceCube's construction.

CHAPTERS
0:00 The building that hides a detector
0:30 Reveal the instrument
1:04 Why neutrinos are so hard to catch
1:47 How to build it: hot water and 2 km of ice
2:37 What a detection actually means
3:36 2017: a message and a direction
4:52 Back to the ice

SOURCES
IceCube - detector overview: https://icecube.wisc.edu/science/icecube/
NASA GCN - IceCube mission page: https://gcn.nasa.gov/missions/icecube
IceCube FAQ: https://icecube.wisc.edu/about-us/faq/

IceCube timeline: https://icecube.wisc.edu/about-us/icecube10/timeline/

NASA - Fermi traces source of cosmic neutrino: https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasas-fermi-traces-source-of-cosmic-neutrino-to-monster-black-hole/

MEDIA CREDITS
Antarctic field footage: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center. Videography courtesy of Kelly Brunt, Adam Greeley, Matthew Means and Chris Simmons. Filmed for the 88-South Traverse; not IceCube construction footage. Source audio not used. https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/13206/

items.title: The Explosion That Left No Crater (Tunguska 1908)
title_options: The Explosion That Left No Crater (Tunguska 1908)
items.description:
The Explosion That Left No Crater (Tunguska 1908)

On June 30, 1908, a powerful explosion over central Siberia flattened about 2,000 square kilometers of forest, yet no giant impact crater was found. Using NASA Landsat imagery from 2024, a photograph from Leonid Kulik's 1929 expedition and labelled reconstructions, we look at the evidence for an airburst: a cosmic object releasing its energy in the air, kilometers above the ground.

No camera recorded the 1908 event. Every moving image of the explosion in this video is a reconstruction, not footage. Energy and size figures are model-dependent estimates. The Chelyabinsk 2013 sequence is a schematic, not footage of Tunguska.

CHAPTERS
0:00 The explosion that left no crater
0:45 Tunguska from orbit today
1:05 June 30, 1908
1:43 Landscape-scale destruction
2:16 Kulik's search
3:19 The missing crater
3:48 How an airburst works
4:50 How powerful, how high
5:26 What the trees reveal
6:07 Other ideas, still debated
6:37 Chelyabinsk, 2013
7:07 Back to the forest today

SOURCES
NASA Earth Observatory - A Cosmic Explosion over Siberia (2025): https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/a-cosmic-explosion-over-siberia-154488/
NASA History - 115 Years Ago: The Tunguska Asteroid Impact Event: https://www.nasa.gov/history/115-years-ago-the-tunguska-asteroid-impact-event/
NASA NTRS - Tunguska workshop summary (2019): https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20190002302

MEDIA CREDITS
Satellite image: NASA Earth Observatory image by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey (Landsat 8 OLI, July 6, 2024). Epicenter and Lake Cheko positions follow NASA Earth Observatory's labels.
1929 photograph: Leonid Kulik expedition, May 1929, as published by NASA Earth Observatory; public domain (Wikimedia Commons: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tunguska_Ereignis-1.jpg ). Shown in black and white, cropped and zoomed.
Forest, airburst, map, timeline, globe and city scenes: original Orbital Atlas illustrations, marked RECONSTRUCTION / ILLUSTRATION, not to scale.
Narration: AI voice (ElevenLabs). Sound: original synthesized wind and low rumble, no music.
NASA does not endorse this video.

items.title: NASA Touched an Asteroid. Then It Started Sinking.
title_options: NASA Touched an Asteroid. Then It Started Sinking.
items.description:
NASA Touched an Asteroid. Then It Started Sinking.

On October 20, 2020, NASA's OSIRIS-REx spacecraft reached down to asteroid Bennu to grab a sample. The surface barely pushed back: the sampler arm sank nearly half a meter (about 1.5 ft), and it was still sinking when the back-away thrusters fired. Here is the contact second by second, why Bennu's surface behaved like a ball pit, the mark it left behind, the leaking sampler head, and the 121.6 grams that made it back to Earth.

CHAPTERS
0:00 The touch that kept sinking
0:38 Why go to Bennu
1:16 Nobody was steering
1:47 The contact, second by second
2:48 Why the surface barely resisted
3:38 The mark left at Nightingale
4:22 Second problem: a leaking sampler head
4:52 121.6 grams and what scientists found

WHAT YOU ARE SEEING
- Real images: SamCam and NavCam 2 photo sequences (sped up or shown at their published cadence, not real-time video), spacecraft camera images of the sampler head and capsule (October 2020), PolyCam before/after images of Nightingale (March 7, 2019 / April 7, 2021), NASA video of the capsule on the ground (September 24, 2023).
- NASA animations: the data-driven reconstruction "Thirty Seconds on Asteroid Bennu", the TAGSAM animation and the Moon vs. Bennu comparison. On-screen times are approximate times from contact in NASA's reconstruction; slowed sections are marked.
- NASA data model: surface height change at Nightingale.
- Orbital Atlas illustrations (marked ILLUSTRATION): signal delay diagram, cross-sections of the loose surface, sampler head cutaway, capsule return, mass chart, symbolic molecule icons in the chemistry summary (icons, not chemical structures). Symbolic, not to scale.
- Sound effects are sound design, not recordings from Bennu. No original NASA audio or music is used.
- Narration: synthetic voice (ElevenLabs).

SOURCES
- NASA (2022-07-07), Surprise - Again! Asteroid Bennu Reveals its Surface is Like a Plastic Ball Pit: https://www.nasa.gov/missions/surprise-again-asteroid-bennu-reveals-its-surface-is-like-a-plastic-ball-pit/
- NASA SVS (2022-07-07), Thirty Seconds on Asteroid Bennu: https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/20360
- NASA SVS (2023-09-25), OSIRIS-REx Tags Asteroid Bennu Videos: https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/31244

items.title: NASA Lost Contact With Voyager 1. Then the Signal Came Back.
title_options: NASA Lost Contact With Voyager 1. Then the Signal Came Back.
items.description:
NASA Lost Contact With Voyager 1. Then the Signal Came Back.

In October 2026, NASA's Deep Space Network listened for Voyager 1 two days in a row and heard nothing. Before engineers sent a troubleshooting command, the signal came back on its own. Here is what happened, what the spacecraft had been doing, and why every question to Voyager now takes two days to answer: on November 18, 2026, Voyager 1 is about one light-day from Earth.

CHAPTERS
0:00 The signal that went quiet
0:22 Listening for Voyager: October 18, 19 and 20
0:38 The clue: a thruster switch
0:56 Why troubleshooting takes 48 hours
1:27 One light-day from Earth
1:42 A different kind of repair
2:14 49 years in space
2:30 Interstellar space since 2012
2:40 One conversation, two days

WHAT YOU ARE SEEING
- NASA animations and data visualizations of Voyager and its trajectory (NASA Scientific Visualization Studio), the Pale Blue Dot image and a Deep Space Network antenna photo (NASA/JPL-Caltech).
- Orbital Atlas illustrations (marked SCHEMATIC / ILLUSTRATION): signal paths, clocks, the time-distance diagram, thruster and power diagrams. They explain the story; they are not NASA data or NASA screens.
- ATLAS is an animated host character, not a real person, and was not present at any real event shown.
- Music and sound effects are original sound design, not recordings from space.
- Narration: synthetic voice (ElevenLabs).

SOURCES

- NASA, Voyager 1: What Is a Light-Day?: https://science.nasa.gov/mission/voyager/voyager-1/voyager-1-what-is-a-light-day/

items.title: NASA Astronauts Saw Five Flashes on the Far Side of the Moon
title_options: NASA Astronauts Saw Five Flashes on the Far Side of the Moon
items.description:
NASA Astronauts Saw Five Flashes on the Far Side of the Moon

During the Artemis II lunar flyby, Orion passed behind the Moon and lost radio contact with Earth, as planned. While Mission Control waited, the crew watched the dark lunar surface and marked where they saw brief pinpricks of light, likely meteoroid impact flashes. Here is where Orion was, what the crew could see, what an impact flash is, and how their color-coded notes became evidence for NASA's lunar science team.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Five pinpricks of light
0:10 Where Orion was
0:22 Behind the Moon, out of contact
0:40 Why the dark Moon matters
0:54 What an impact flash is
1:11 Reading the crew's notes
1:30 Eyes and cameras
1:50 Contact restored
2:03 Why stare into darkness

WHAT YOU ARE SEEING
- NASA video from Artemis II (crew aboard Orion, Mission Control, the lunar science team), NASA simulations of the crew's window view, NASA's flight-path animation, NASA's impact flash animation (labelled ANIMATION) and the crew's annotations on a simulated view of the Moon from NASA's preliminary lunar science report.
- No impact flash was filmed for this video. The flash animation is NASA's; our scale pictures are marked ILLUSTRATION.
- The notebook cover and its sketched marks are a concept illustration, not observed locations.
- Orbital Atlas schematics (marked SCHEMATIC, not to scale): Earth, Moon and Orion positions, the radio blackout, the atmosphere comparison and the timeline.
- ATLAS is an animated host character, not a real person, and was not aboard Orion.
- Music and sound effects are original sound design, not recordings from space.
- Narration: synthetic voice (ElevenLabs).

SOURCES
- NASA, Artemis II Preliminary Lunar Science Report: https://science.nasa.gov/feature/artemis-ii-preliminary-lunar-science-report/
- NASA, Artemis II crew Moon photo annotations: https://www.nasa.gov/image-article/artemis-ii-crew-moon-photo-annotations/
- NASA SVS 15103: https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/15103/
